data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma is a category error: 'probability' in Popper's sense refers to logical frequency or propensity, while 'preference' refers to methodological utility; conflating them creates a pseudo-problem.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'methodological utility' inevitably collapses into 'subjective probability' in the mind of the agent.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the separation between logical status and practical action is unsustainable in complex, real-time decision environments.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the concept of 'propensity' itself is shown to be incoherent or dependent on inductive assumptions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper defines probability objectively (propensity). Corroboration is a historical report of a theory's performance. Preference is a forward-looking methodological stance. The mechanism is 'semantic compartmentalization.' When Popper says corroboration isn't probability, he means it doesn't change the logical propensity of the theory being true. When he says we should prefer it, he means it is the most useful tool for the current state of inquiry. The 'smuggling' charge fails because it tries to map a methodological rule onto a logical calculus where it was never intended to reside. The cost is accepting a fragmented view of rationality where logic and action operate under different rules.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
